On behalf of the United States of America, I congratulate the people of Liechtenstein on your National Day.

items.title: Trump Administration Announces Additional Support Following Colombia Earthquake
items.author: Office of the Spokesperson
items.summary:
Office of the Spokesperson

Trump Administration Announces Additional Support Following Colombia Earthquake

Media Note

August 14, 2026

The Trump Administration is leading a life-saving response to the devastating 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck Colombia on August 10.  Today, the Department of State is announcing $11 million in additional humanitarian assistance, bringing the total U.S. assistance following the earthquake to $26.5 million.  The Department is also leveraging support from the U.S. Department of War (DoW) U.S. Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) to transport relief supplies from the Department of State’s Miami prepositioning warehouse to Colombia.  The State Department continues to coordinate with Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella and the Colombian government to assess and respond to earthquake-related needs.

Additional Life-Saving Humanitarian Assistance

The Department of State is mobilizing a total of $26.5 million – including today’s announcement of an additional $11 million – in humanitarian food, health, protection and shelter assistance, in addition to post-earthquake structural assessments through trusted partners, including Catholic Relief Services (CRS), the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, the International Organization for Migration (IOM), Miyamoto International, UNICEF, the UN World Food Program (WFP), and World Vision.  Of the initial $15.5 million in assistance announced on August 11, $3 million provided through CRS draws from the previously announced CRS global assistance award.  Additionally, as part of the Department’s $3.8 billion contribution to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) announced earlier this year, the United States provided $200 million to the Colombia Pooled Fund, which OCHA can use to address earthquake-related needs as well as preexisting humanitarian needs in Colombia.

Leveraging DoW Support to Deliver Relief Supplies

The Department of State is also leveraging support from SOUTHCOM to transport relief supplies from the Department’s Miami prepositioning warehouse to Colombia.  The first of the planned flights is scheduled to depart Homestead Air Force Base in Florida’s Miami-Dade County today, carrying shelter and water and hygiene supplies.  Upon arrival in Colombia, IOM and WFP will receive the supplies and oversee last-mile distribution to Colombians impacted by the earthquake.  Today’s flight will include hundreds of Starlink kits that will provide reliable, high-speed internet to many humanitarian organizations and the Colombian government to facilitate their relief efforts.  The delivery of these kits will occur in coordination with the State Department, following the disaster response coordination memorandum of understanding signed between Starlink and the Department earlier this summer.

Arrival of Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) Technical Support Teams

In coordination with the Colombian government, the Department of State activated and deployed two USAR technical support teams from the fire departments of Fairfax County, Virginia, and Los Angeles County, California.  These teams arrived in Colombia on August 12 and are providing USAR coordination, communications, and structural engineering support to Colombian government-led search and rescue operations.

Supporting Americans in Colombia

The Trump Administration has no higher priority than the safety and security of Americans.  The State Department is working tirelessly to provide consular assistance to U.S. citizens and their families in the affected areas.  Americans in Colombia should enroll in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) at STEP.state.gov to receive safety and security updates from the U.S. Embassy.  They should follow @TravelGov and @USEmbassyBogota on social media for the latest information.  The Department’s Bureau of Consular Affairs maintains a call center for Americans seeking information or assistance in connection with the Colombia earthquake: call 888-407-4747 from within the United States or Canada, or +1 202-501-4444 from all other locations.

items.title: Joint Statement on the Sixth Meeting of the Joint Security Coordination Mechanism for the Peace Agreement Between the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Republic of Rwanda
items.author: Office of the Spokesperson
items.summary:
Office of the Spokesperson

Joint Statement on the Sixth Meeting of the Joint Security Coordination Mechanism for the Peace Agreement Between the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Republic of Rwanda

Media Note

August 13, 2026

The text of the following statement was released by the Governments of the United States of America, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Republic of Rwanda, the State of Qatar, the Republic of Togo (as the African Union mediator), and the African Union Commission on the occasion of the sixth Joint Security Coordination Mechanism meeting held this week in Geneva, Switzerland.

Begin text.

On August 12-13, 2026, representatives from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Rwanda (the Parties), along with the United States, Qatar, Togo (as the African Union mediator) and the African Union Commission convened the sixth meeting of the Joint Security Coordination Mechanism (JSCM) at the U.S. Mission in Geneva, Switzerland.

The DRC and Rwanda agreed to advance two initiatives to strengthen monitoring and verification of Washington Accords implementation on the ground. The parties requested that the United States consider these two initiatives and provide feedback at the next JSCM. The parties agreed to a trilateral planning conference in October 2026 that will culminate in a revised Operations Order guiding their coordinated efforts.

The African Union Commission presented on the outcomes of the African Union High-Level Meeting in Gaborone, Botswana, held July 24-25, 2026.

The DRC presented its Disarmament, Demobilization, and Reintegration (DDR) Plan for the Forces Démocratiques de Libération du Rwanda (FDLR) and responded to questions from JSCM members. Following the DRC’s presentation, the JSCM held a virtual session with the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the DRC (MONUSCO) to draw on its operational experience conducting DDR in the region.

The Governments of the DRC and Rwanda expressed their appreciation to the United States, Qatar, Togo, and the African Union Commission for their support throughout the peace process and agreed to reconvene for the next JSCM on September 16 –17 in Geneva.

End text.

items.title: Second Session of the U.S.-Nigeria Joint Working Group to Address Nigeria’s Country of Particular Concern Designation
items.author: Office of the Spokesperson
items.summary:
Office of the Spokesperson

Second Session of the U.S.-Nigeria Joint Working Group to Address Nigeria’s Country of Particular Concern Designation

Media Note

August 13, 2026

Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs Allison Hooker hosted the second Joint Working Group (JWG) with a Nigerian delegation led by Nigerian National Security Advisor Mallam Nuhu Ribadu in Washington on August 12, 2026.  The engagement builds on progress made since the first session held in Abuja, Nigeria, on January 22, 2026.

Discussions centered on three priority areas: protecting Christian communities in Nigeria’s Middle Belt, holding perpetrators of violence accountable by strengthening judicial and security institutions, and military-to-military cooperation.  Under Secretary Hooker and the Nigerian delegation reviewed progress on internally displaced persons’ (IDP) resettlement to their ancestral homes, counterterrorism prosecutions, and combatting the financing of terrorism.  The JWG identified continuing challenges, including reports of civilian fatalities and gaps in humanitarian expenditure transparency.  Discussions on military-to-military cooperation continue today at the Pentagon.

The United States noted Nigeria’s reported efforts to date, including the prosecution of hundreds of Boko Haram and Islamic State-West Africa (ISIS-WA) suspects, expansion of judicial capacity, and recruitment and training of 50,000 additional police officers.  Both sides acknowledged that more work lies ahead, particularly with supporting IDPs.  The two sides also discussed continued cooperation on countering terrorism financing, biometric information sharing to support accountability measures, and law enforcement capacity building through the Department’s Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs (INL) and Bureau of Counterterrorism (CT).

Under Secretary Hooker separately met with NSA Ribadu to further advance bilateral priorities and reaffirm the United States’ commitment to working with Nigeria to protect Christian communities and to deepen joint security cooperation.

For media inquiries, please submit questions here.

items.title: Joint Statement from the International Contact Group for the Great Lakes (ICG)
items.author: Office of the Spokesperson
items.summary:
Office of the Spokesperson

Joint Statement from the International Contact Group for the Great Lakes (ICG)

Media Note

August 13, 2026

The United States, Belgium, Canada, Denmark, the European Union, France, Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom, as members of the International Contact Group (ICG) for the Great Lakes region, chaired by France, issue the following statement regarding the disarmament, demobilization, and cantonment protocol signed between the Congolese authorities and the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda-FOCA (FDLR).

Begin Text:

The ICG takes good note of the announcement made on 28 July by the DRC government, that a faction of the FDLR formally accepted and signed a protocol on their disarmament, demobilization, and cantonment.

The ICG urges the Congolese authorities to promptly develop an operational plan and a realistic timeline to implement an effective FDLR neutralization in line with obligations signed in the Washington Agreements and the Disengagement of Forces/Lifting of Defensive Measures of Rwanda (CONOPS) of October 31, 2024, and the Washington agreement of June 27, 2025.

The ICG notes the crucial importance that the Congolese Government implements the protocol. It therefore also urges the Congolese government to clarify the mechanisms for combating impunity, as referred to in the protocol, and to work with MONUSCO as a key partner in implementation. The ICG further underscores that any colocation or operational collaboration with elements of the FDLR is fundamentally at odds with the commitments made in the Washington Accords.

At the same time, the ICG is ready to welcome any concrete steps forward taken by either the DRC or Rwanda, following commitments made in the framework of the peace process.

The ICG urges all parties to the Washington Accords and Doha Framework, as well as the various mediation efforts, including those of the African Union, to continue their efforts to implement the commitments made.

The ICG reminds the parties of their obligation to protect civilians, to comply with Security Council resolutions 2773 and 2808, including full respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, and to immediately de-escalate the situation.

The ICG also recognizes the prisoner exchange agreement between the DRC and the AFC/M23 as a vital confidence-building measure to de-escalate tension and foster trust between the warring parties. In this regard, the ICG commends the recent transfer facilitated by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) of individuals released by Congolese authorities to AFC/M23, which is a step in the right direction.

The group also calls on all parties to honour their obligations to respect international humanitarian law and to guarantee full, safe, and unimpeded humanitarian access in order for essential aid to be delivered to those in need.

End Text.

items.title: Ending DEI Ideology in the Foreign Service
items.author: Office of the Spokesperson
items.summary:
Office of the Spokesperson

Ending DEI Ideology in the Foreign Service

Fact Sheet

August 13, 2026

The U.S. Department of State has put an end to the ideologically extreme and discriminatory diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) agenda, restoring merit, rigor, and accountability to the Foreign Service and refocusing training on practical diplomatic skills that serve the common interests of the American people.

Ending DEI Ideology in the U.S. Foreign Service

The DEI agenda was embedded in the institutional culture of the Foreign Service during the previous administration. DEI objectives and materials shamefully denigrated the United States, derided Americans of certain backgrounds, and distracted from legitimate foreign policy objectives that serve the American people. Under the Trump Administration, the State Department has eliminated DEI ideology from Foreign Service training to better uphold the highest standards of American diplomacy.

A thorough internal review revealed that objectionable DEI content was previously incorporated in training curricula and other personnel materials, including in the following ways:

  • A DEI reading list for Foreign Service instructors included extreme Critical Race Theory texts, including Robin DiAngelo’s “White Fragility and the Rules of Engagement,” “In Defense of Looting,” “How White Women Tears Oppress People of Color,” “The Case for Reparations,” and “How to be Anti-Racist in Humanitarian Aid,” among other texts that promoted division among America’s diplomats, insulted the American people, and damaged mission effectiveness.
  • Guidance on how Foreign Service Officers could fulfill a DEI promotion metric urged diplomats to discuss DEI issues with high-level foreign government counterparts, demonstrate “allyship,” and “acquire more DEIA knowledge on your own” instead of depending on “others from historically marginalized groups to teach you.”
  • A DEI toolkit for Foreign Service instructors included trainings on discussing “white privilege” and “systemic racism” in foreign languages. Trainings included “Let’s Talk About Black Lives Matter in Bangla,” a discussion on systemic racism in Urdu, an exercise on integrating “Black Lives Matter” terminology into Hebrew lessons, and a roleplaying exercise on “race and racism” in the United States and foreign countries.
  • A vocabulary list of DEI terms instructed State Department officials to avoid using accurate terminology such as “illegal alien” when discussing unlawful immigration, referring to it as a “problematic term.”
  • Foreign Service course instructors received an “Inclusivity Guide” that provided learning materials and DEI guidance to adhere to in the workplace, including a pamphlet promoting “international pronoun day,” rules on incorporating fanciful “non-binary pronouns” (invented terms such as “Ze,” “Zir,” and “Zirs”) into course materials, and an article discussing ways to cope with being accused of a microagression, among other materials that were divisive, damaging to morale, and prejudicial to mission effectiveness.
  • A day and a half of dedicated DEI instruction was added to the five-week Foreign Service orientation course and a full day on DEI was incorporated into a five-day Foundations of Public Diplomacy course.
  • State Department officials were instructed to practice “microaffirmations” to mitigate their “unconscious bias” and “microaggressions.”

America’s diplomats are the nation’s first line of defense against hostile powers, terrorists, deadly narcotics smuggling, illegal immigration, and other threats to the safety, security, and prosperity of the American people. The State Department is implementing modernization reforms to the Foreign Service and invites all Americans with the skill and spirit to represent our nation around the world to apply to join the U.S. Foreign Service.

items.title: State Department Establishes Task Force to End Birth Tourism
items.author: Office of the Spokesperson
items.summary:
Office of the Spokesperson

State Department Establishes Task Force to End Birth Tourism

Fact Sheet

August 12, 2026

Under President Trump and Secretary Rubio’s leadership, the Department of State is using all available tools to defend the integrity of U.S. citizenship, ensure nonimmigrant visas are used only for their lawful and intended purposes, and prevent their exploitation through birth tourism. As President Trump has made clear, citizenship is not a commodity to be acquired through the calculated exploitation of U.S. immigration laws. The Department of State is working closely with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to combat birth tourism and protect the integrity of the U.S. immigration system. 

New Birth Tourism Prevention Task Force 

To maximize the success of this comprehensive effort, the State Department has established a Birth Tourism Prevention Task Force.

  • The Birth Tourism Prevention Task Force reviews the activities of visa holders worldwide to identify instances of birth tourism, take action to revoke visas of those who engage in or facilitate it, and dismantle the networks that profit from this abuse.
  • The Task Force addresses the abuse by analyzing and connecting information held across the Department and other federal agencies, including the DHS.
  • Thanks to the coordination of the Task Force, the Department of State is addressing birth tourism on a global scale, examining travel histories of individuals from all around the world in order to end this exploitation and abuse.
  • The Birth Tourism taskforce has taken action by revoking more than 600 visas from foreign nationals across the globe to safeguard our nation from this abuse.
  • The Department generally revokes visas when there are indications of a potential ineligibility.
  • The Secretary has broad discretionary authority to revoke visas – and the Trump Administration is committed to exercising that authority to protect the American people and the integrity of our immigration system.

Birth Tourism Has Become a For-Profit Industry 

Facilitators have turned birth tourism into a lucrative, for-profit industry.

  • These facilitators sometimes market themselves as doulas, midwives, or wellness advocates while openly advertising “birth in the U.S.” services, visa coaching, and hospital arrangements.
  • Some forge medical documents or coach clients to conceal their true travel purpose and avoid paying hospital bills, with online marketing promising clients “automatic citizenship” and “a future without borders.”
  • The facts are clear – birth tourism is a pervasive practice that involves nationals from countries spanning every region of the globe.
  • The Department is taking action to dismantle these networks and hold all participants accountable.

Birth Tourism Fraud 

The work of the Bureau of Consular Affairs Task Force and consular officers at U.S. embassies and consulates around the world is exposing widespread patterns of deception.

  • Foreigners who willfully misrepresent the purpose of their travel or entry into the United States may be permanently ineligible for a U.S. visa or entry to the United States.
  • The Department has uncovered patterns that illustrate the lengths some applicants will go to circumvent our laws in order to secure U.S. citizenship for their children – and potentially for themselves in the future.
  • One couple used a conference and a vacation trip to go shopping as cover stories to give birth to two children in the United States, lying about their travel purpose in two separate visa applications. On the second occasion, the couple concealed that they had a child.  The visas have been revoked.
  • In another case, a foreign government official requested a visa to travel on behalf of her government for just one week, but instead stayed three months and gave birth in the United States before departing. The Department revoked the visa.
  • Another traveler applied for a visa to go on vacation in Orlando and instead traveled to Los Angeles and gave birth five days after arrival. The Department revoked the visa.

Citizenship is not a commodity to be acquired through calculated exploitation and evasion of the immigration laws.  Foreign nationals who abuse the visa system, and those who help them do so, may lose their visa, their access, and their future in the United States. This is only the beginning.

items.title: Pax Silica AI Assistance Project NOFO
items.author: Office of the Spokesperson
items.summary:
Office of the Spokesperson

Pax Silica AI Assistance Project NOFO

Media Note

August 12, 2026

At the Second Pax Silica Summit in Washington, D.C. on June 25-26, Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg announced a new Pax Silica AI Assistance Project to more efficiently and rapidly move high-value AI inputs through Panama.  The Department has published a competitive Notice of Funding Opportunity for this ambitious new platform that has the potential to transform how trusted partners transship rapidly critical goods that power the AI economy of the 21st century.  Working with Congress, the Department seeks to commit up to $50 million in foreign assistance funding to strengthen global AI supply chain security by developing an AI supply chain credentialing and provenance platform that expedites the shipping of semiconductors, AI infrastructure, critical minerals, and related products in participating Pax partner countries and economies. We are putting our resources behind our vision and demonstrating that trusted partnership is backed by real investment.

The Pax Silica AI Assistance Project would begin as a pilot, implementing an AI supply chain credentialing platform with Panama’s ports and customs authorities. If the pilot with Panama is successful, a second phase of the project would expand the geographic reach of these platforms to other Pax Silica countries and economies.

Interested bidders are encouraged to apply for this Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) at Opportunity Listing – Pax Silica Artificial Intelligence Assistance Project before the NOFO closes on August 20.  This deadline is firm and will not be extended.  Any questions from potential bidders regarding the NOFO should be directed to PaxFund-NOFO-DL@state.gov.

items.title: Joint Statement by Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy and Secretary of State Marco Rubio: United States to Serve as Secretariat of the Geneva Consensus Declaration
items.author: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
items.summary:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Joint Statement by Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy and Secretary of State Marco Rubio: United States to Serve as Secretariat of the Geneva Consensus Declaration 

Press Statement

August 12, 2026

As the Secretariat of the Geneva Consensus Declaration returns to the United States, we express our deep appreciation to Hungary for its exceptional stewardship. Hungary has faithfully safeguarded the Declaration and its principles, and we are grateful for its leadership and commitment to expanding the Declaration’s signatories.

The United States will carry this work forward through a whole-of-government effort led jointly by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the U.S. Department of State. The Secretariat will be housed within the Office of Global Affairs at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.

Established in 2020, the Geneva Consensus Declaration, led by the United States, began as a joint initiative with a few like-minded countries. Today the group has grown to include more than 40 signatories.

The Declaration has four main objectives: to secure meaningful health and development gains for women; to protect life at all stages; to defend the family as the fundamental unit of society; and to work together across the UN system to realize these values.

The Trump Administration is committed to supporting families, promoting women’s health, and protecting children at all stages of life. Investing in women’s health and well-being saves lives, allows women and girls more opportunities, and protects the family as the fundamental unit of society.

items.title: Secretary of State Marco RubioWith Katie Miller of The Katie Miller Podcast
items.author: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
items.summary:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Washington, D.C.

Thomas Jefferson Room

Secretary of State Marco RubioWith Katie Miller of The Katie Miller Podcast

Interview

August 11, 2026

QUESTION:  Hi, everyone, and welcome to this week’s episode of The Katie Miller Podcast.  We’re at the State Department today, joined by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and his beautiful wife Jeanette.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  It’s good to be with you, finally.

QUESTION:  I know.  So excited.  So you briefly just said you’d have a career in podcasting after this.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  I don’t know yet.  I mean, I’m going to see how this one goes and then we’ll play it from there.  But it won’t be about politics.  It might not even be about foreign policy.

MRS RUBIO:  Sports.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Sports, yeah.  College football, cultural things.

QUESTION:  You’ve joked about your career after politics.  What do you think it would be?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  I don’t know, obviously.  I hadn’t even thought about that yet.  But I love the sports stuff, so I’d be – I’d love to be involved in, like, the intersection of sports and culture.  But basica lly, whatever pays the most.

QUESTION:  Anything to do the Fox News?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  (Laughter.)  I’d like to do the commercials on Fox.  That’s one of our inside jokes is I’m always – I always look at the commercials that are running on Fox, whatever they’re advertising, like a rain gutter or whatever, and I’m like, I think I could be the pitch – if I could line two or three of those, two or three of those alone, I’m probably set for a while.  So I think I could be the pitchman, like, whatever William Devane is selling.  (Laughter.)  He’s got his big thing going.  So I have my eye on that.  We’ll see.

QUESTION:  Jeanette doesn’t do many interviews, so thank you for doing this.  What did you think about his move from being a senator to Secretary of State?  Were you on board the second he brought it up or did you take some convincing?

MRS RUBIO:  No, I was on board.  I was because of everything that’s going on in our country.  And so I was totally on board when he told me that this is something he was considering.

QUESTION:  What’s easier, being a Senate spouse or being the wife of the Secretary of State?

MRS RUBIO:  I think they’re both different.  I would say being a Senate spouse is probably easier just because there were less events; there were things that I didn’t have to do, being now in D.C.  But they’re both – they were both – they’re both great.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  You asked the wrong question.  You have to ask which one was more fun.

QUESTION:  Which one was more fun?  (Laughter.)

MRS RUBIO:  Being – now.  Being a Secretary of State spouse.

QUESTION:  You get a lot of praise for how you hold yourself and the events that you’ve gone to with Marco.  Most recently there was a viral moment where you handed him your phone in India.  (Laughter.)

MRS RUBIO:  I did.  I did.

QUESTION:  What other things does he carry for you besides your phone?

MRS RUBIO:  Oh, my gosh, a lot of things.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  I’ve had makeup.

MRS RUBIO:  Yes, my makeup.  Yeah, because those purses are so small, so you can’t fit a lot of things in there.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  But it looks weird.  Like, if the outline comes out, you have, like, this – people think I walk around with, like, mascara and compact on my pockets.

MRS RUBIO:  Which is why I —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  It’s like, this guy is really vain.  (Laughter.)

MRS RUBIO:  So I learned that I do it in public so he can’t say no.  (Laughter.)

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah.  But I’ve been fully loaded.  There’ve been times where I have a phone and then I have, like, the compact thing here and then the other makeup here and then the little crayon thing —

MRS RUBIO:  No, that’s not true.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Not crayons, but the liner or whatever.

MRS RUBIO:  Not true.  Usually it’s one or two things.

QUESTION:  Does he carry a ring light every so often?  Is he a good photographer?

MRS RUBIO:  Oh, no.  No, no, no.  No.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  What do you mean, like cell phone photography?

MRS RUBIO:  Like —

QUESTION:  Yeah.  Are you good at cell phone photography?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Oh, she has one of those light things too.  Remember?  I had one of those in my pocket one time.

MRS RUBIO:  I did, but I don’t ever really use it.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  And I thought it was like a foreign listening device.  (Laughter.)  Like, oh, my God, they bugged me, what is this thing in my pocket?  And then I realized that was, like, a light you attach to your phone.  But for about 10 seconds I thought I had been, like – a tracking device had been dropped in my pocket by somebody, so —

QUESTION:  What’s on your playlist right now?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  That’s a really good question.  I haven’t been able to update my playlist, but I love – I say this like – people think whatever.  I love a lot of electronic music because it fuses classical, increasingly it does country music.  So I like a lot of the remixes of, like, songs that you’ve heard over the – there’s this EDM mix of Ring of Fire which is really good.  So I like that stuff.

So I listen to a little bit of everything except for, like – I don’t hate it, okay?  I’m not against it. I’m not anti-country music, but that’s not my thing.  She loves it.  She loves country.

MRS RUBIO:  I love country music.  I do.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  I think it’s just very sad.  Most of the songs are about, like, somebody whose wife and dog left them and so —

MRS RUBIO:  Well, that’s not true.  You need to listen to more Morgan Wallen and others because that’s not true.

QUESTION:  Who’s your favorite rapper?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Of all time?

QUESTION:  Yeah.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  I mean, just from an artistic standpoint – and obviously, he never lived long enough to know what he would’ve turned into, but Tupac was very, very talented, I thought.  And he was actually very talented, not just – people forget.  I mean, he was, like, trained to be an actor as well.  I think he went to, like, that school in New York or in Baltimore.  I forgot exactly where he went to high school, but he went to a artistic high school, and you can see that later on when he played a number of roles in a number of movies over the years, including the one with Janet Jackson, that he was a good actor.  He was a good lyricist in terms of the lyrics that he wrote.  He left a lot of music, some of which has still not been released, that his family holds.  So I thought he was a very talented person, primarily because I think he was a narrator more than anything else of a certain point of view and lifestyle, or upbringing and worldview.  So I think of all time he’s probably my favorite.  There’s a lot of other very talented people.

But – but yeah, some of the modern – like, the younger people that are out there now I’m really not as familiar with because the whole hip-hop genre has changed quite a bit.  And it’s not for the worse or the better, I’m just saying it’s changed.  But the ’90s were great.  The only problem with the ’90s is they all – they’re like – these people, like, were shooting at each other, like, for real.  Like, it wasn’t just in their lyrics, especially when the whole Death Row thing and the East Coast thing developed over time.  So I grew up in that era, and it’s a little different than it is now, even though some of these guys still get in trouble.  But anyway —

QUESTION:  What’s life like as Secretary of State and National Security Advisor?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Every day is different, right?

MRS RUBIO:  Yeah.

QUESTION:  So you wake up in the morning, and what happens when you’re both here in D.C.?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, it depends what time you wake up in the morning because the way the world is, like, sometimes you’ll – “wake up in the morning” means 2:30 because there’s something going on at, like – it’s prime time somewhere else.  So sometimes that’s what wakes you up.  It also depends, although we’ve been pretty busy on the national security front because of Iran and before that other things, but there’s no single typical day.  Typically weekends are just a little slower, obviously but – and then the President has an insane work schedule.  Like, he works every day, all day.  You guys know that, too.  So he doesn’t really have, like, days off or vacation time.  There is really no slow time when it comes to national – international affairs.

So no day is typical, but generally speaking, if I had to plan a day, I would start – I start here at the State Department in the mornings and then try to be over at the White House before or shortly after noon and when the President really gets humming.  And then obviously – or sometimes in the mornings he does a lot of foreign leader calls, so I’m on a lot of those calls in the morning.  Those are sometimes as early as 7:00 a.m.  So —

QUESTION:  When you wake up at 2:30 in the morning, do you wake Jeanette up as well?  And then what do you do during that time?  Do you go back to sleep?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  No, she might hear the phone ring.  Or she might hear it —

MRS RUBIO:  Yeah, I hear the phone ring but I don’t wake up.  No.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  She doesn’t – no.  All that —

MRS RUBIO:  He gets up when he needs. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah, I’ll go to another room.  I’m not going to – but – and that doesn’t happen every day.  I don’t want to exaggerate, but it happens.  And then sometimes the phone call is just to tell you can you go down to your classified phone or whatever so you can get the news from there.  So then you know it’s, like, for real.  So anyway.

QUESTION:  I don’t think most people realize that when you were a senator, Jeanette stayed back in Florida.  What was that decision like, and how is that working now with his schedule?

MRS RUBIO:  So the decision was made because we figured we wanted to keep our kids with the same day-to-day routine and their environment and not change anything.  So that was the compromise that we made. 

I think the kids are older now.  They’re all graduated from high school and now they’re in school, in universities.  So now it’s different.  I mean, now it’s easier for me because I’m able to now be a part of more of what he’s doing, and I think it was the best decision.  It was the best decision for our kids.  I  mean, he would come down also when he was a senator, down on weekends, and I think he liked it as well because it kept him grounded around his constituents, wouldn’t you say?  And also see his family.

MRS RUBIO:  Oh, my gosh.  He would do —

MRS RUBIO:  Or need counseling.  (Laughter.)

SECRETARY RUBIO:  No, no, no, no.  None of  my kids – they’ve become desensitized.  So, like, nothing surprises them.  And so —

MRS RUBIO:  Okay.  Yeah, well, yes, they’re – they’re ready.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah.

MRS RUBIO:  According to Marco Rubio’s theory.  But – but no, I mean, we had a lot of fun and we have four kids.  They all had different personalities, and when Marco would come down it would cause a great stir.

QUESTION:  It’s been the summer of babies in the West Wing.  What was Marco like when you guys were first having kids?  Do you have any good stories for having babies?

MRS RUBIO:  He was good.  He was good.  When he – he would help me especially as they multiplied, right?  So when – so I would get my sleep and he would put on the alarm, and he would – when he was doing his speeches he would wake up, he would get the baby, right, and he would feed the baby at night sometimes for me.  I mean, the majority of the time I did it, but he would help me a lot.  He did.  That he was very good at.

QUESTION:  What was your favorite age of parenting?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Look, there are times – like, you know when you’re on your phone, like, you’ll get those memory pictures that pop up?  And I always tell people, like, I would give a lot of money for one more day, like just 24 hours of that era.  And so that was fun when they were little because you remember that part of them.  But I also enjoyed, especially with the boys in some respects, the sort of the adolescent high school years because they were involved in sports and I had a chance to be a part of some of that.  So that was fun.

But I think every stage, every season of life has its own – like, I always tell people one day you’ll look back at this and say these are the good old days, and that’s true of every stage. 

MRS RUBIO:  It’s true.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  You look back at every time, and when you’re in the middle of it you don’t realize it.  And then —

MRS RUBIO:  And it goes by so fast.  It really does.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Ten years from now, we’re going to be looking back at these times and say, oh, remember we were in Washington and the kids this, that, and the other.  So I think you almost – probably one of the things that I learned over time is you try to appreciate the moment that you’re in right now, because that moment’s not going to come back.  And every stage and every – every season of life has its things that you should enjoy.

So I don’t know if I had a favorite.  They were all very different.  And it was easier when they were little because they kind of didn’t have schedules and you’d just scoop them up and take them where you’re going.

MRS RUBIO:  Yes.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  As they got older, they had activities and things they had to do.

MRS RUBIO:  And they wanted to do your – they wanted to do everything you were doing.

QUESTION:  What’s the most surprising thing about being Secretary that nobody warned you about?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  The interesting thing is – again, it’s the – it’s a different job, but when you’re in the Senate for 14 years doing foreign relations, you know a little bit about how the place happens and works.  I think that the breadth and scope of the State Department, and power in particular, it wasn’t surprising.  It was revealing to me because you sort of perceived it, but you didn’t realize, like, there’s a lot that other agencies do that requires the State Department to either okay or sign off on or initiate.  And so I think that’s surprising to me. 

The other – I wouldn’t say it’s surprising, but I came to appreciate it more, is a lot of the customer service work we do, because people think of the State Department as, like, diplomacy, and it is.  But we also do passports.  We also help people all over the world in the consulates and embassies – American travelers somewhere and they get in trouble or have a bad situation, and we help them. 

So I think you come to appreciate, like, the professionalism of the people that do that work and how valuable it is, because for a lot of Americans their only interaction ever with the State Department will be the day they lose their passport, or the day they realize they have a cruise on Saturday morning and it’s Friday and they haven’t – they didn’t renew their – they didn’t renew their passport.  So I think I’ve come to appreciate more that part of the job that the State Department does. 

QUESTION:  You’ve mentioned that this job is a bit more fun than the last job.  What’s been the most surprising part of that for you?

MRS RUBIO:  Oh, my gosh, 250, those fireworks – I mean, they were spectacular.  That was – I would say that was great.

MRS RUBIO:  Than retrievers.

MRS RUBIO:  Oh, my gosh.  (Laughter.)

SECRETARY RUBIO:  And so – and anyway, and my dog just walked into their living room and looked around, realized I’m in the wrong house, and turned around and walked out.  So they’ve had some experience over there.  But I think the dogs are attracted to his house because of the cats.  They’ll never catch ‘em, but the –

MRS RUBIO:  So yes, he entered.  He was sitting there watching TV, and he entered their house.  And he’s like – they’re like, what is this?  (Laughter.)  And we were dying of embarrassment.  But yes, so our dog does open the door, many doors.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Now, the flip side of it is that one of Pete’s cats – oftentimes I’ll get home at night and the cat is just sitting on my porch and just looks at me, like, what are you doing here?  (Laughter.)  Like that kind of attitude about —

MRS RUBIO:  Yeah, yeah. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  It’s an arrogant cat.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  To be honest, it’s a very arrogant cat.

MRS RUBIO:  There’s a lot of kids.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Because the cat is on my porch acting, like, what are you doing in my house?  And it’s like no, your house is two doors down.  (Laughter.)  But the cat just looks at you.  It doesn’t even – usually a cat, you approach it and it takes off.  This one does not take off running.

MRS RUBIO:  Yeah, he’s not scared of anything.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  He just sits there.  The tail’s going on like this, and he’s just staring at you, like, what’s up?  (Laughter.)  And I’m like, this cat’s amazing.  I don’t even know the name of this cat.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  And – but I have long been on this UAP thing, and now I’ve sort of surrendered that portfolio to someone else who you know well who’s very much in charge of the UAP issue.  Just – again, it’s not – what I say is I don’t know who it is, I don’t know what it is, but there are things flying over our military installations and they’re not ours, and we should look into this, be serious about it.  And I did that for a long time in the Senate, and it had two benefits. 

The first is that, obviously, it’s a legitimate topic.  And the second is, whatever the news of the day was, it was controversial.  And if a reporter comes up to you and you say to them, “Look, I don’t have time for these questions about politics.  Do you realize there’s things flying over our airspace, we don’t know what they are?”  And the reporter’s like, “Oh, what do you know?  Tell me more.”  So it was extraordinarily effective as a diversionary tactic in addition to.  Now, that said, it’s also a very legitimate topic that we should be covering.

So I don’t call it a conspiracy.  I don’t know if I – I don’t know the answer to any of it.  I’m just asking the questions about we should know what’s flying over our airspace.  But I don’t think that’s a conspiracy theory as much as it is just – it can be, in some sense, because people do believe we’re covering something up.  And I assure you, like, in this administration, if we knew, like, the President would be all over it.  Like, there would be a primetime address.  He would —

Anyway.  (Laughter.)  This whole thing’s off the rails.  You’re not going to be able even to air this thing.

MRS RUBIO:  That movie is crazy.  It’s crazy, but yeah.

QUESTION:  How often do you talk to President Trump?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Every day.  Multiple times. 

QUESTION:  What’s been the latest at night and the earliest in the morning?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Early in the morning?  He’ll start working the phones at or around 6:00 a.m.  And at night?  I don’t know, 2:00, 2:30, maybe.  So – that I can recall.  But I don’t think there’s – I mean, if he’s working on stuff, he’s working on it.  But I would say probably the latest I can recall, like, fielding a call from him is around – shortly after 2 o’clock, and probably the earliest is before – just after 6:00.

QUESTION:  What’s the best joke he’s ever told you?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  The best joke?  He’s not like a – people – he’s funny, but he’s not a joke teller, right?  Like, he’s not – he just – he tells – he’s a great narrator.  And he’s got incredible – people don’t realize, like, he’s been a public figure for almost half a century.  Like, he has – he met a lot of people, and he’s gotten to know a lot of people over the years.  And so he has great stories going back to, like, celebrities in the ’80s and people he interacted with and people he was around.  So I don’t know of one in particular that stands out, but I’m fascinated by these stories because some of these are stories that go – I mean, he knew Michael Jackson.  He knew – he knew everybody.  He knew everybody at some point or another.  He had interacted with everybody.  He’s just got great stories.  If you ask him about somebody, he’ll go back and tell you about them.  And it’s a pretty amazing life he’s lived.

QUESTION:  When he approached you to be secretary of state, is that something you were seeking or did that just happen?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah, I don’t know if “approach” is the right term.  He just basically called me and told me, you’re going to be the secretary of state.  (Laughter.)  It wasn’t presented as, like, an option – (a) you can stay in the Senate, or (b) you can —

QUESTION:  And you said okay.  Did you think about it? 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Not really.  I mean, I think I’m – there had been some sense that that – something like that could happen.  But it was the middle of the campaign and I wasn’t going to raise it, and he wasn’t going to talk about it.  But I think it was maybe, like, 48 hours after – or maybe 72 hours – it wasn’t long after the election.  He just basically called me and said, hey, this is what – I think he had even already Truth-posted it, and then he told me about it.  So it was – (laughter) – and I was happy to do it, and I was honored to do it.  I’m not saying that.  I’m just saying it generally wasn’t presented as, like, “Hey, would you be interested in…”  It was more like, “Hey, you’re going to be,” and I said okay, here we go.

QUESTION:  You’ve been one of the toughest voices on Cuba forever.  We captured Maduro out of Venezuela.  Is Cuba next?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  I think Cuba – I am confident that Cuba, by the time this administration’s over, before this administration ends, will be on an irreversible path towards a much different future.  Obviously, like anything else, especially something like this, I always tell people, like, you can’t have something in place for 70 years, it grows roots, and then think overnight you’re just going to rip out the whole thing and put something brand-new into the ground.  There’s a transition that has to happen and a process to get there.  Eastern Europe is instructive of that.  You saw it took countries in Eastern Europe three to five years to truly become what we know them to be today.  Poland is probably the best example.

So I think Cuba will be on that path, well along that path.  It has to be.  But certainly under this administration, given the priority it’s given Cuba, I – I – like, you never guarantee anything, but it’s certainly a priority for us because it’s in our national interest.  I remind people, at the end of the day, like, I work for the United States of America.  I care about Cuba, obviously I have a personal connection to it, but I don’t work for Cuba; I work for the United States.  And I believe it’s in the national interest of our country to have a Cuba that’s safe and stable and aligned with the U.S. – the same feeling I have about Venezuela as well.

QUESTION:  When the Maduro raid happened, what was it like leading up to that?  What was he like?  Was he nervous?  What was the vibes?

MRS RUBIO:  I don’t know.  That’s a good question.  I think I just see him busier.  I just see him more on the phone.  He’s just – he’s thinking.  But he’s – I would say he’s cool and collected.  I mean, I – that’s – I wouldn’t say he isn’t, but —

MRS RUBIO:  Oh, yeah, okay.  What a beautiful answer.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  But the true answer is – and I – here’s where I messed up that answer, okay?  Because here’s the thing:  The day would actually start much earlier.  The greatest show on television today in America is College GameDay.  Great show.  Starts around 10 or 11, and that leads into noon, and then the noon game, and then there’s a 3:30 game, and then there’s a – so I messed – and the ideal – like, this is a crazy weekend; it would never happen.  So I’m just putting this out there.  But you could start at 10:00 a.m. on Saturday, run the whole college football day, sleep for a few hours, then you wake up and then you’re into NFL GameDay, then you’ve got the 1 o’clock game, the 4 o’clock game, the NBC game that night.  That is an incredible weekend, in my opinion, in my view.  Obviously, I don’t believe that will ever – I will ever achieve this; certainly not in the next two and a half years or what have you.  But – and your audience probably doesn’t care anything about what I just said, but I’m just telling you that that would be a crazy day.  But that’s never going to happen.  Right?  Maybe?

MRS RUBIO:  Well, you never know.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  You never know.

QUESTION:  Would you be okay with him watching that much football, or do you sit with him and watch the football, or are you off doing something else?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  No, she doesn’t watch.

MRS RUBIO:  No, no.  I don’t.  I mean, I’ll sit and watch some, but no. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  She’ll watch a game if my son is in the game.

MRS RUBIO:  Exactly.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  The one that’s at Florida. 

MRS RUBIO:  Exactly. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Or – that’s about it, actually.  (Laughter.)  That’s about it.

QUESTION:  How long did it take for you to figure out the State Department?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Figure out the State Department?

QUESTION:  Yeah.  Like, navigate it, figure it all out, unpack it all.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, I think that’s still a learning process.  I mean, along the way we’ve also done a – what I think was a very important reorganization of it, to bring it back more to its core principles.  I think we did a lot of things that previous secretaries of state – many of whom will never admit it – wish they could have done in terms of, like, bringing foreign aid together with foreign policy so that they’re both pushing in the same direction.

QUESTION:  Did any of your predecessors give you advice coming into the job?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  A few.  I mean, I don’t know “advice” is the right term; I think they gave me their impressions.  But I think so much of what we do here is dependent on the times in which you live.  If you were secretary of state in the middle of the Cold War, or secretary of state post-9/11, that’s a very different world from what we’re facing right now.  So I think there’s some things they can give you advice on in terms of, like, how they managed their schedule and how – but ultimately the secretary of state works for the president.  And so a lot of what you do in this job, and what this place does, should be geared and aligned and built around what the president – who the president is.  And so a – a Department of State under President Trump is – should look different than it looks under the next president, what it’s going to look like under the next president, or previous presidents.  It should be a reflection of the foreign policy direction that the current president wants to take it.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Oh, me, big-time. 

MRS RUBIO:  (Laughter.)  Oh, please.  That’s not true. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Are you kidding me?  But I’ll say almost anything to move past it, whatever it was.  Like, I – she has great memory and stuff, and I don’t.  So for example, like –

MRS RUBIO:  (Laughter.)  That is not true.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  — she can recall something that happened in 1999; on September of ’99, do you remember when you said or did this?  And I’m like, no, I – actually I don’t remember this.  And so she has an incredible sort of catalogue of – (laughter) – grievances that she’s able to use at appropriate times.  As I, on the other hand, I – my preference is generally to move on from things quickly.  Like, you deal with it off – you get mad, you get whatever, and then you just move quickly on it. 

So – but I don’t know.  I mean, look, you asked that question about marriage.  Marriage is not a – unfortunately people watch a lot of movies and stuff, and they think that marriage is about, oh, just two people that are always happy and always – I mean, it’s life.  You make —

MRS RUBIO:  Right.
